docs.title: open-hydra
docs.text:
Hydra translates evidence into data points with a simple, modular framework. It is a minimal framework that provides simple interfaces for investigative tasks such as conflicting data points, source provenance, and visualization-compatible data.

  • An archive is a plain folder of records, rules and review decisions; hydra-ctl pack zips it into one .hydra file
  • Tracking which sources conflict on individual data points
  • Tree generation of hierarchies (i.e., family, employment, organizational)
  • Resolves most data fields into directed graphs

Hydra reads and writes standard FollowTheMoney JSON, as Aleph and OpenSanctions use it, and its own variant that writes links as names instead of ids.

Warning

Hydra is in Alpha mode. Core components are still under development and may change before the stable release.

To try it, install it and follow the quickstart. How Hydra works explains what a build does, and the command reference covers every command and flag.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Hydra needs Python 3.11 or later. Install hydra-ctl from GitHub with uv or pip:

uvpip 
uv tool install git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra

pip install git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra

Then run hydra-ctl on its own to see the command list.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
To get the latest version:

uvpip 
uv tool install --reinstall git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra

pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall --no-deps git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra

docs.title: Removing
docs.text:
uvpip 
uv tool uninstall open-hydra

pip uninstall open-hydra

To use Hydra from an AI assistant, install hydra-mcp as well.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This walks through one archive from start to finish. You need hydra-ctl installed and some FollowTheMoney JSON records.

docs.title: No data yet? Try the demo
docs.text:
Every example in this guide uses the Pollard demo archive, built from the public record of one espionage case. To build it yourself:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra
hydra-ctl init demo --name "Pollard case" --prefix pollard
cp open-hydra/examples/demo/collections/*.json demo/collections/
cp open-hydra/examples/demo/.hydra/rules/positions.yaml demo/.hydra/rules/
mkdir -p demo/.hydra/sources/entries
cp open-hydra/examples/demo/.hydra/sources/entries/*.json demo/.hydra/sources/entries/
cd demo
hydra-ctl build
hydra-ctl tree "task force"

docs.title: 1. Create an archive
docs.text:
hydra-ctl init case --name "My Case" --prefix mc
cd case

init creates the folder from the built-in template. Hydra Archives explains what is in it.

docs.title: 2. Add records
docs.text:
Copy your .json files into collections/, or load one with import, which checks that it reads as records first:

hydra-ctl import ~/exports/people.json --format ftm

docs.title: 3. Build
docs.text:
hydra-ctl build      # merge, place and write .hydra/parsed/
hydra-ctl check      # problems in the files

docs.title: 4. Look around
docs.text:
hydra-ctl details                  # one-screen summary
hydra-ctl tree                     # the org chart
hydra-ctl claims "Some Name"       # where each value came from
hydra-ctl sources                  # which documents cite what

docs.title: 5. Answer the open questions
docs.text:
hydra-ctl todo       # count what is open
hydra-ctl review     # answer them one by one

Reviewing shows what each question looks like.

docs.title: 6. Share it
docs.text:
hydra-ctl pack                         # one portable .hydra file
hydra-ctl export --format graphml      # for Gephi, yEd, Cytoscape

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
Every command is hydra-ctl <command> [<dir>] [options]. Leave out <dir> and the command uses the active archive (see activate) or the current folder.

Run hydra-ctl alone for the list, or hydra-ctl <command> --help for one command's options.

hydra-ctl details                         # one-screen summary
hydra-ctl tree                            # the org chart
hydra-ctl tree "task force"                # start at a search
hydra-ctl positions                       # the position ladder and titles nothing takes
hydra-ctl claims "Jonathan Jay Pollard"  # read the claims for "Jonathan Jay Pollard"
hydra-ctl sources                         # which documents cite what
hydra-ctl hints                           # image and badge rules, with hit counts
hydra-ctl check                           # problems in the files
hydra-ctl todo                            # open questions
hydra-ctl review                          # answer them one by one

docs.title: Commands and what they write
docs.text: Command Does Writes init Creates an archive, or opens a .hydra file into one The new folder activate, deactivate Set the archive to use when none is given .hydra-activate in this folder import Loads FtM JSON (standard or Hydra's), or a CSV or GraphML export, as a collection The collection file, then rebuilds build Compiles the collections and sources into a build .hydra/parsed/ and collections/manifest.json check Lists the problems in the archive's files, without building Nothing details One screen of records, types, tree size and open questions Nothing tree Draws the record tree, from a type, a relationship or a search Nothing positions Draws the position tree and the titles no position takes Nothing claims Shows where each value of an entity came from Nothing node find Lists the records closest to a value Nothing sources Lists the sources, and which entities cite each Nothing todo Counts what the last build needs a person to decide Nothing review Asks the open questions one by one verdicts.yaml, then rebuilds answer Records one decision, for scripts verdicts.yaml, then rebuilds reset Removes decisions, after backing them up verdicts.yaml and a backup, then rebuilds stubs Lists names that links point at but no record has, and graduates one verdicts.yaml, then rebuilds pack, unpack Turn an archive into one .hydra file, and back The .hydra file, or the folder export Writes the archive for other tools The output file or folder collections Lists collections and their id prefixes, and changes one collections/manifest.json, then rebuilds defaults Checks, switches off or restores the default config files hydra.yaml, or the restored files hints Lists the image and badge rules, and links an image file by one .hydra/resources/ and hints.yaml, then rebuilds

docs.title: Explore
docs.text: These commands read the last build. None of them write anything.

docs.title: Searches
docs.text:
tree, claims, sources and node find understand the same kinds of word, in any order and any capitalisation:

Word Does Example A type, such as person, organization or company Keeps that type and its subtypes (organization includes companies) hydra-ctl claims person anne A relationship (tree only): ownership, membership, employment, directorship, occupancy or family Draws the chart along it hydra-ctl tree family employment sources Adds the sources of what the command returned hydra-ctl claims pollard sources Anything else The search, matched against names first and then other fields hydra-ctl node find pollard

Several search words make one search, so claims jonathan jay and claims "jonathan jay" are the same. A word may match the start of a name: jon finds Jonathan Jay Pollard.

Option Does --names Searches names and ids only --no-text Searches every field except free text (notes, descriptions)

search in hydra.yaml sets how far searches look when neither flag is given.

docs.title: check
docs.text:
hydra-ctl check
hydra-ctl check --format json

See the output of each example

Lists every problem in the archive's files (rules, params, records and decisions) as errors, warnings and infos, without building. It exits with status 1 when there is an error.

  code                        level   found by   count   file
  direction.both-ends-above   info    check          1   .hydra/schema/direction.yaml

  code                        where       message
  direction.both-ends-above   Occupancy   both ends (holder, post) are in `above`; the target, post, is the parent

             check   old build
  errors         0           0
  warnings       0           0
  info           1           3
Option Does --format <text / json> Chooses how to print it (text by default)

docs.title: details
docs.text:
hydra-ctl details
hydra-ctl details htest.hydra --format json

See the output of each example

One screen with the archive's name, when it was built, its collections and prefixes, records and entities by type, tree size, open questions and issues. It warns when files changed since the build, and never builds.

Option Does --format json Prints it as data

docs.title: tree
docs.text:
hydra-ctl tree
hydra-ctl tree person
hydra-ctl tree "task force"
hydra-ctl tree family
hydra-ctl tree family employment
hydra-ctl tree organization sources

See the output of each example

Draws every record once, under one parent, like an org chart. A record's other parents are listed under it, so nothing is hidden.

Task Force 168 (PublicBody)
└── Jonathan Jay Pollard (Person) — Analyst
      also  Anti-Terrorist Alert Center                   Employment   analyst
      also  Naval Ocean Surveillance Information Center   Employment   research analyst
      also  Navy Field Operational Intelligence Office    Employment   analyst

When there is a reason the other parent isn't the drawn one, the line ends with it: rejected (you said no in review), cycle (it would make a loop) or earlier (its dates don't overlap the drawn one). With no word, both parents hold at once and the chart shows one.

Command Draws tree The whole chart tree person From each person not below another person tree "task force" From the records the search names tree family Only family links, and only the people in them tree family employment Both kinds, the first one a record has deciding its parent tree organization sources The chart, then the sources of everything drawn

docs.title: Relationship charts
docs.text:
A relationship word draws only links of that kind. Every record at either end of one is drawn, each labelled with its link, and records with none are left out (the header counts them).

Records joined by these links are drawn together, with a blank line between unconnected groups, so one family reads as one block.

Anne Henderson-Pollard (Person)
Jonathan Jay Pollard (Person)
  also  Anne Henderson-Pollard   Family   wife   sideways

For family, the relationship text decides the direction. It describes the relative from the person's side, so father, mother or parent puts the relative above the person, and son, daughter or child puts the person above the relative.

A child's line reads from the child's side ("child (father)" means the record says father). Anything else, such as spouse, sibling, uncle or in-law, stays sideways and is listed under the record's person on a "sideways" line.

Relationship charts only change what is displayed. Nothing is rebuilt or saved, and a parent you rejected or one that would make a loop is never used.

Option Does --read <declared / generic> Uses your hierarchy rules (declared, the default) or the generic ones only --stubs Also draws the names no record has where their links would put them, as if each were graduated (nothing is saved; see stubs) --format <text / json / mermaid> Chooses how to print it --ascii Uses plain ASCII lines instead of box drawing --vertical, --lateral, --direction, --singletons Mermaid only; see below

docs.title: Mermaid
docs.text:
hydra-ctl tree --format mermaid > chart.mmd
hydra-ctl tree --format mermaid --vertical --direction LR
hydra-ctl tree family --format mermaid

--format mermaid prints the same chart as a Mermaid flowchart, which renders on GitHub, in mermaid.live and in most Markdown editors. Every way of choosing what to draw (a type, a search, a relationship, --read, --stubs) works the same.

Line Means Solid arrow --> The parent the record is drawn under, labelled with the role Dotted arrow -.-> One of its other parents (the also lines), labelled with the role Dotted line -.- A sideways link, such as Associate or Family, labelled with its wording %% no links: comment The records left with no line, which Mermaid doesn't draw

Labels come only from the records, never from your review choices.

docs.title: Mermaid options
docs.text:
Mermaid lays out every line as if it went down, so sideways and other-parent lines pull records onto the wrong rows. On anything bigger than a small search, draw one kind of line at a time.

Option Draws Use it for --vertical Only the solid lines The hierarchy itself, the org chart --lateral Only the dotted lines Who else each record is tied to --singletons Records with no line as boxes, instead of listing them in the %% no links: comment Keeping every record on the chart after --vertical or --lateral drops its lines --direction LR Left to right instead of top-down (TD, the default) Wide, shallow trees

docs.title: positions
docs.text:
hydra-ctl positions
hydra-ctl positions --tree --nodes
hydra-ctl positions --unplaced
hydra-ctl positions --format mermaid

See the output of each example

Draws the position ladder from the hierarchy rules: each position under the one above it, with the titles that count as it listed underneath. Then it lists the titles found in the data that no position takes, so you can see what the rules are missing.

Analyst
  titles   analyst
           research analyst
  records  Jonathan Jay Pollard   Person
Associate   outside
  titles   associate
           close associate
           contact
Leader
│ titles   boss
│          leader
│          head of organization

outside marks a position that is off the ladder, implied one only the rules imply, and ^ a position met a second time. Problems in the rules, such as a position placed under one that isn't defined, are listed at the end.

position works as well. To change the ladder, see Defining Hierarchies.

Option Does --tree Shows only the position tree --unplaced Shows only the titles no position takes --nodes Lists the records holding each position under it --read <declared / generic> Uses your hierarchy rules (declared, the default) or the generic ones only --format <text / json / mermaid> Chooses how to print it; mermaid draws the position graph --ascii Uses plain ASCII lines instead of box drawing

docs.title: node find
docs.text:
hydra-ctl node find pollard
hydra-ctl node find person jay
hydra-ctl node find per-w3v2f7z7pe --field id

See the output of each example

Gives the records closest to a value, each with a score, and says which field matched.

score   name                     schema   id                       position   parent           matched
1.00    Jonathan Jay Pollard     Person   pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe   Analyst    Task Force 168   weakAlias  Pollard
0.93    Anne Henderson-Pollard   Person   pollard:per-jbcv7nwbwb

An equal name or identifier scores 1.00, a name holding all the words 0.90 or more, part of an id 0.85, another field equal to the value 0.80, and another field holding its words 0.75. Anything else is scored by how close it is to a name, so typos still find.

Option Does --field <any / name / id / identifier / value> Chooses where to look (any by default) --type <type> Does the same as a type word --limit <n> Shows at most that many (10 by default, 0 for all) --min <score> Hides anything lower (0.6 by default) --read <declared / generic> Chooses which read to search --format json Prints it as data

docs.title: sources
docs.text:
hydra-ctl sources
hydra-ctl sources sella
hydra-ctl sources person --uncited
hydra-ctl sources damage
hydra-ctl sources --format json

See the output of each example

Draws a tree per source, the source on top. Each source entry in .hydra/sources/entries/ shows its type, publisher, id and link, with the entities that cite it underneath.

Each entity's line names the field that cites the source. It names the record too when the entity was merged from several records and the citation came from one of the others.

A document's pages sit under it, and whoever cites a page sits under that page. Documents that are part of the data, such as a case file and its pages, are listed apart from the source entries, and entities that cite nothing are counted.

In the demo, everything traces to one source entry, the damage assessment:

  The Jonathan Jay Pollard Espionage Case: A Damage Assessment (Document)   Foreign Denial and Deception Analysis Committee, Director of Central Intelligence   pollard:doc-v9g25vcmkx
  └── Aviem Sella (Person)   sources   pollard:per-6q0b4zamfq
  …
Command Draws sources Every source sources sella Only the sources the entities the search names cite, with only those entities under them (names first, other fields only when no name matches) sources person The same for every person sources person --uncited The same, and also names each person citing nothing, so you can see what still needs a source sources damage Searches the sources themselves (id, title, publisher and link) when no entity matches, and draws each with everything citing it

The word sources after claims, node find or tree draws the same for just what that command returned. Sources covers how they are stored.

Option Does --uncited Names each entity citing nothing, not just how many --format <text / json> Chooses how to print it (text by default) --ascii Uses plain ASCII lines instead of box drawing

docs.title: Review and decide
docs.text: These commands answer the questions a build leaves open, and save the answers in .hydra/review/verdicts.yaml. Reviewing shows what each question looks like.

docs.title: todo
docs.text:
hydra-ctl todo
hydra-ctl todo --list
hydra-ctl todo --list placements

See the output of each example

Counts the questions the last build left for a person, by kind. --list shows each question with the id that answer takes.

Option Does --list [kind] Lists the questions; with merges, references, placements, stale, contradictions or verdicts, only that kind --format json Prints it as data

docs.title: review
docs.text:
hydra-ctl review
hydra-ctl review --only merges

See the output of each example

Asks the open questions one at a time. Each starts with what kind of question it is (Merge, Reference, Placement, Stale decision, Contradiction or Decision problem) and a detail such as the fields in conflict.

Then it asks "Which is better?" with the alternatives numbered and the current one marked "now". A merge with conflicting fields opens on just those fields; Tab shows the rest.

[2/2] Placement · Membership (several parents)
  Aviem Sella
  …
Which is better?
  1  under Israeli Air Force     pollard:org-ez802bp11f   now
  2  under New York University   pollard:org-f8xs95cwk2
  ? not sure   u undo   q quit

Merges offer one entity or two, references the records a name could mean, and placements the parents a record could sit under. Stale decisions and contradictions come after.

Press a number to answer, ? or Enter to leave it open, u to undo the last answer and q to stop. A placement made by the position rules also offers a, to keep every placement the same rule made.

Each answer is saved at once, and the archive is rebuilt once at the end.

Option Does --only <kind> Asks only merges, references, placements, stale, contradictions or verdicts --no-build Skips the rebuild at the end

docs.title: answer
docs.text:
You probably won't use answer. But an AI agent might.

hydra-ctl answer merge-3f2a… confirm
hydra-ctl answer place-17bd… reject
hydra-ctl answer ref-520d… 2
hydra-ctl answer cap-pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe "Jonathan Pollard"
hydra-ctl answer place-17bd… clear

See the output of each example

Records one decision, for scripts. The ids come from todo --list.

Id Takes merge-… confirm, reject or clear. It is saved with its evidence, so it comes back as stale if that changes place-… confirm, reject or clear ref-… A candidate number, a record id, none or clear cap- and a record id One of the entity's names (not an alias), or clear

An entity has several names once records are merged. In the demo, with a press file added that calls him "Jonathan Pollard", confirming the two are one man makes cap-pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe "Jonathan Pollard" valid.

Option Does --no-build Saves the decision without rebuilding

Removes decisions from .hydra/review/verdicts.yaml. It says what will go, writes a backup beside the file, waits for Enter, then rebuilds.

To clear a single decision, use answer with clear.

docs.title: stubs
docs.text:
hydra-ctl stubs
hydra-ctl stubs graduate "Lakam"
hydra-ctl stubs graduate "Israeli Ministry of Defense" --as PublicBody
hydra-ctl stubs drop "Lakam"

See the output of each example

A stub is a name that link fields point at but no record has, such as an owner that names a company nobody wrote a record for. With no action, stubs lists each one: how many links name it, from which fields, and the most specific type all of those links can point at. Then it lists the names already graduated.

graduate turns a stub into one entity, so every link with that name points at it, and rebuilds. It takes the type the links fit unless --as names another.

drop undoes a graduation. Both are saved as decisions in verdicts.yaml, so reset removes them too.

To see where the stubs would land before graduating any, use tree --stubs.

Option Does --as <type> Graduates the name as that type --no-build Saves the decision without rebuilding --format json Prints the list as data

docs.title: hints set
docs.text:
hints set links an image to every entity a match picks, without editing YAML by hand. Give it portrait, thumb (an icon) or logo, the image, and one or more of these:

Option Picks --schema <type> Entities of that type and its subtypes --position <position> Entities in that position --titled <text> Entities with a stated title that contains it (a regular expression; case and accents are ignored) --name <name> The entity's name (aliases are not read)

When you give several, all of them must hold. Anything wider (aliases, other fields, any:) goes into hints.yaml by hand; see Images and badges.

The image is copied into .hydra/resources/ (portraits/, icons/ or logos/) unless it is already inside it. A different file with the same name is never overwritten: rename yours, or point at the one already there.

The rule is added to the end of hints.yaml, quoted correctly and with your comments left alone. If check finds a problem with it (an unknown type or position, or a bad pattern), the file is put back as it was.

After rebuilding, it says how many nodes the rule reached, or that it matches nobody yet.

See the output of each example

Loads records into the archive as a collection, from the same formats export writes. Copying a file into collections/ yourself and running build does the same for ftm and hydra-ftm; import checks the file reads as records first, names the collection and rebuilds.

Format Is ftm Standard FollowTheMoney JSON: a list, {"entities": [...]}, or JSON lines, as Aleph, OpenSanctions and other FtM tools write it. FtM's proof is read as sources hydra-ftm The same with links written as names, as export --format hydra-ftm writes it csv The folder export --format csv writes (nodes.csv and edges.csv) graphml The file export --format graphml writes

A graph carries each entity's id, type and name, and its links. Each relationship edge becomes the relationship (with its role and dates), and each link-property edge the property.

Other fields are not in a graph, so they don't come back. The tree and open merges (placedUnder, sameAs) are left out too; a build works them out again.

ftm and hydra-ftm files are copied as they are, and a graph is written as FtM JSON lines. The collection takes the file's name (case.ftm.jsonl becomes case, case-graph/ becomes case).

Option Does --format <format> Says what the file is: ftm, hydra-ftm, csv or graphml --name <name> Chooses the collection's name --force Replaces a collection of that name --no-build Imports without rebuilding

docs.title: build
docs.text:
hydra-ctl build
hydra-ctl build htest --force

See the output of each example

Reads every file in collections/ and .hydra/sources/entries/, merges records that are the same entity, places them, and writes .hydra/parsed/. It prints a summary of records, claims, nodes, merges, placements and references by status, and issue counts.

When nothing has changed since the last build, it prints that summary again without building.

Standard FtM data works as it comes. A link field that holds a record's id (as in owner: ["NK-p1"]) is followed by that id and shown as the record's name, and the id is kept for export.

Option Does --force Builds even when nothing changed --no-prefix Keeps record ids as written, without prefixes --verbose Also prints the full summary: claims, reads and the review ledger

docs.title: pack, unpack
docs.text:
hydra-ctl pack
hydra-ctl pack htest -o case-one.hydra
hydra-ctl unpack case-one.hydra

See the output of each example (and unpack)

pack writes the archive as one .hydra file, a zip with a checksum for every file, including the last build. The same archive always gives the same bytes, and the parse cache is never included.

unpack checks every file and refuses paths that would leave the folder. init with a .hydra file does the same as unpack.

Option Does -o, --out <file> Chooses where to write the pack (the archive's name by default) --no-parsed Leaves the build out for a smaller file; it builds on first use --force Replaces an existing file

docs.title: export
docs.text:
hydra-ctl export --format ftm
hydra-ctl export --format csv -o graph
hydra-ctl export case-one.hydra --format graphml

See the output of each example

Writes the archive for other tools, and reports what it wrote:

Exported Pollard-case as csv to ~/cases/graph
  entities   nodes   edges   unlinked relationships   ftm schema
        45      26      54                        0   65c772987032
Format Is ftm Standard FollowTheMoney JSON lines, for Aleph, OpenAleph and nomenklatura. Links hold record ids, sources are written as FtM's proof, and referents are kept hydra-ftm The same in Hydra's own form, with links as the names the records wrote. It can go back into a collection csv nodes.csv and edges.csv with export.yaml, for Kùzu, Neo4j and Gephi. Every relationship is an edge, plus the chart's chosen parent with its status graphml The same graph in one file, for Gephi, yEd and Cytoscape

Every export is stamped with the FtM schema hash from hydra.yaml. import reads all four formats back in.

Option Does --format <format> Chooses the format (required) -o, --out <path> Chooses where to write it (named after the archive, here, by default) --read <declared / generic> Chooses which read to export --force Replaces an existing output

docs.title: Hydra Archives
docs.text:
Hydra uses its own archive format to hold everything needed to merge records, build hierarchies and link sources and media to entities: the data, the rules that shape it, and the decisions made while reviewing it.

Warning

Everything here is in alpha and will very likely change, including where things are installed. Hydra will not drift from its principle: a modifiable, portable configuration travels with the data, with defaults provided and methods kept consistent.

An archive is a folder. hydra-ctl init <folder> creates one there from the built-in template.

case/
├── hydra.yaml                      the archive's name, id prefix and FtM schema hash
├── collections/                    your records
├── session/                        reserved; not used yet
└── .hydra/                         managed by hydra
    ├── sources/entries/            the sources your records cite
    ├── rules/                      positions and media rules
    ├── review/                     your review decisions (verdicts.yaml)
    ├── schema/                     the FollowTheMoney schema, params, direction and extension types
    ├── resources/                  icons and media
    ├── parsed/                     the last build
    └── cache/                      parsed config kept between runs

Records and collections and Sources cover the data. Config files covers hydra.yaml, the rules and the schema.

docs.title: session/
docs.text: session/ is reserved for a future feature. Nothing reads it yet: put records in collections/.

docs.title: resources/
docs.text: .hydra/resources/ holds the images that hints.yaml points at.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: Hydra ships generic defaults for the rule and schema files. Only change these if you want to set your own custom hierarchy; defaults shows which ones you have changed and restores them. It doesn't cover the FollowTheMoney schema in .hydra/schema/ftm/; see Config files.

docs.title: The .hydra file
docs.text:
hydra-ctl pack turns an archive into one portable .hydra file: a zip of everything above, with a checksum for every file and the last build included. The same archive always packs to the same bytes, and the cache is left out.

hydra-ctl init case.hydra opens one into a folder. Commands that only read take the file directly.

docs.title: How Hydra works
docs.text: Hydra acts as a compiler. It reads everything in collections/, merges records that are the same entity, places each one in a hierarchy, and turns everything it can't settle into questions for review. The result can be used as a source for display in a UI.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
Instead of strict field adherence, Hydra assumes your fields are correct. It then proposes a set of review tasks to clarify key details, identify conflicts, and automatically merge identical entities.

Your answers are saved in the archive and applied on every later build. If you merged all your claims, you would produce the dataset already in collections/.

hydra-ctl todo counts what is open, by kind:

Kind Asks merges Are these two records the same entity? references Which record does this name mean? placements Which parent should the tree draw this record under? stale A decision's evidence changed. Is it still right? contradictions Do two sources disagree on a value? verdicts A saved decision no longer matches a question. Keep it?

Reviewing shows how to answer each one.

docs.title: Trees
docs.text:
A record can have several parents: the organization it is a member of, the company that employs it, the person it reports to. Hydra draws every record once, under one parent, like an org chart, and lists its other parents under it so nothing is hidden.

Choosing the parent only changes how the tree is drawn. The data in the entity's fields does not change.

docs.title: What a build writes
docs.text:
hydra-ctl build reads collections/, .hydra/sources/entries/ and the rules, and writes .hydra/parsed/:

File Holds generic.json, declared.json The two reads of the hierarchy, one with the generic positions only and one with yours claims.jsonl Every value of every entity, with the record and collection it came from identical.jsonl The merges ledger.jsonl The placements, references and other questions, each with its status parsed.yaml The combined position rules the build used build.yaml The summary: counts, issues, when it was built

Nothing is carried from one build to the next except your decisions. Two builds of the same archive give the same files, byte for byte, and a build that would change nothing is skipped.

.hydra/cache/ keeps parsed config between runs so builds stay fast. It is safe to delete; the next build is just slower.

docs.title: Records and collections
docs.text:
Your collections/ folder holds .json files, each one a collection. A file can be a JSON list of records or JSON lines, one record per line.

Hydra expects each record's id and schema, with its properties, the way FollowTheMoney writes them. Two records from the demo's collections/pollard-damage-assessment.json (the second one's notes are left out):

[
  {
    "id": "per-w3v2f7z7pe",
    "schema": "Person",
    "properties": {
      "name": [
        "Jonathan Jay Pollard"
      ],
      "alias": [
        "Jonathan Pollard"
      ],
      "weakAlias": [
        "Pollard"
      ],
      "sources": [
        "doc-v9g25vcmkx"
      ]
    }
  },
  {
    "id": "mem-tg0re7j07m",
    "schema": "Membership",
    "properties": {
      "member": [
        "Jonathan Jay Pollard"
      ],
      "organization": [
        "Task Force 168"
      ],
      "startDate": [
        "1980-02"
      ]
    }
  }
]

Everything in collections/ is linked. You can copy a file in and run build, or use import, which checks that the file reads as records first.

docs.title: Ids
docs.text:
Every id is written as <prefix>:<id>, so records from different collections never collide. The prefix is the archive's, or one made from the collection's file name; hydra-ctl collections shows them, and the build stores them in collections/manifest.json. Only the first : splits the prefix from the id.

Hydra takes any id made of letters, digits, - and _. The ids in the demo are the form hydra-mcp makes: a three-letter code for the kind of record, an underscore and ten random characters (per-w3v2f7z7pe is a Person, mem-tg0re7j07m a Membership). The id says nothing about the name, so correcting a name never moves it, and the same person in two collections has two ids that a merge question can join. A page of a document is the document's id and ~p4.

The collection's name is its file name, so rename a file before you start reviewing. Afterwards, change its prefix with hydra-ctl collections prefix, so your decisions follow.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
FollowTheMoney treats some fields as pointers to other entities via their id. Hydra uses natural field values as a container: the linked entity's name.

Here is the demo's Membership above as each export writes it. Both are JSON lines, one record per line, shown pretty-printed:

FtM (export --format ftm)Hydra (export --format hydra-ftm) 
{
  "datasets": [
    "pollard-damage-assessment"
  ],
  "id": "pollard:mem-tg0re7j07m",
  "properties": {
    "member": [
      "pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe"
    ],
    "organization": [
      "pollard:org-ctk7r6bt77"
    ],
    "startDate": [
      "1980-02"
    ]
  },
  "schema": "Membership"
}

{
  "datasets": [
    "pollard-damage-assessment"
  ],
  "id": "pollard:mem-tg0re7j07m",
  "properties": {
    "member": [
      "Jonathan Jay Pollard"
    ],
    "organization": [
      "Task Force 168"
    ],
    "startDate": [
      "1980-02"
    ]
  },
  "schema": "Membership"
}

Both carry the prefixed id, and the collection as FtM's datasets. Only the links differ.

Hydra reads either form. An id is followed exactly and shown as the record's name, and the id is kept for export. A name that fits more than one record becomes a reference question in review.

docs.title: FtM fields that carry over
docs.text: FtM's proof is read as sources, and export --format ftm writes it back as proof. Upstream referents (ids another tool merged into a record) are kept, so the entity can be found by any of them.

docs.title: Stubs
docs.text: A stub is a name that link fields point at but no record has, such as an owner that names a company nobody wrote a record for. stubs lists them and can graduate one into an entity.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
.hydra/sources/entries/ holds the material your data comes from: one record per source, usually an FtM Article or Document with a title, publisher and link. The demo's one entry, with some fields left out (its id is made from the file's contentHash, so one file is one id wherever it is added). Each file is a JSON list, like a collection:

[
  {
    "id": "doc-v9g25vcmkx",
    "schema": "Document",
    "properties": {
      "title": [
        "The Jonathan Jay Pollard Espionage Case: A Damage Assessment"
      ],
      "publisher": [
        "Foreign Denial and Deception Analysis Committee, Director of Central Intelligence"
      ],
      "publishedAt": [
        "1987-10-30"
      ],
      "fileName": [
        "2007-010-doc1.pdf"
      ],
      "mimeType": [
        "application/pdf"
      ],
      "contentHash": [
        "e5acaf72330a527a867c71615f220e61cb4f148e"
      ]
    }
  }
]

A record cites its sources by id in its sources field. The link lives once, on the source entry, never repeated on the records.

Relationships (Ownership, Membership and the like) cite nothing; the entities they join carry the sources.

docs.title: Two kinds of document
docs.text:
A source entry is where content came from: a Wikipedia page, a news article. It belongs in .hydra/sources/entries/.

A document in the data is part of the content itself: a case file and its pages that the investigation is about. It belongs in a collection, like any other record.

Neither appears as a box in the tree; both show up as evidence on the records that cite them.

docs.title: Looking at sources
docs.text:
hydra-ctl sources draws what cites what, and the word sources after claims, node find or tree lists the sources behind just that result:

hydra-ctl sources sella

sources

  entities   1

  entries

  The Jonathan Jay Pollard Espionage Case: A Damage Assessment (Document)   Foreign Denial and Deception Analysis Committee, Director of Central Intelligence   pollard:doc-v9g25vcmkx
  └── Aviem Sella (Person)   sources   pollard:per-6q0b4zamfq

  uncited    0

docs.title: Sourcing one value at a time
docs.text:
A source in FtM is cited by a whole record, not by one of its fields, so Hydra can say which record cites a source but not which value the source supports.

To source values one by one, write one record per source with only what that source says. The build merges them, and claims then traces each value to its own record and source.

docs.title: Defining Hierarchies
docs.text: This guide is for anyone writing .hydra/rules/positions.yaml from scratch, whether a person or an agent working on their behalf. The defaults Hydra ships are deliberately small. Most investigations need their own ladder of ranks, and this is how to build one that Hydra reads the way you mean it.

docs.title: How Hydra builds a tree
docs.text:
Hydra places every record in two steps.

  1. The records decide which organization. A Membership, Employment, Directorship or Ownership record links two entities, and direction.yaml says which end is the parent: the organization above its member, the employer above its employee, the owner above what it owns. When the records give a record several possible parents, review asks you to choose.
  2. Positions rank people inside an organization. Once a record is inside an organization, the position rules decide who it sits under there: a Soldier under the Lieutenant, a Lieutenant under the Underboss. This is what positions.yaml controls.

The position rules only work inside organizations. They never decide which organization someone belongs to, and once you confirm an organization for someone in review, they never move them out of it.

docs.title: Where a record's title comes from
docs.text:
The rules rank a record by its title. Hydra takes the first of these that matches a position:

  1. the role on the relationship that places it (its Membership, Employment, Directorship…)
  2. the role on its other relationships
  3. its own position field

A title matches a position when it equals the position's name or one of its titles, whole. Case and accents don't matter, and punctuation counts as a space:

Role in the record Matches the title Why Vice-President vice president the hyphen counts as a space Vice Président vice president accents are ignored VP vp case is ignored V.P. v.p. only the dots become spaces: "v p" VP of Sales vp of sales only the whole role must match

A record with no role and no position gets no title, so the rules leave it directly under its organization. Hydra never ranks anyone by a title the data doesn't contain.

(direction.yaml can opt in to filling a blank role with edge_positions, but that is off by default for this reason.)

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
Each position is one line:

Position name: {below: [Rank above], titles: [other words for it]}
titles The position's aliases: every wording your data uses for it. The position's own name counts as a title too. below The rank directly above. A record goes under the nearest member of its organization who holds that rank, and if nobody does, under the rank above that. above The same link written from the other side: Underboss: {above: [Lieutenant]} means Lieutenant is below Underboss. Use one or the other, not both, for the same link. outside: true A position beside the organization rather than in it, such as a lawyer or an associate. Outside positions never rank anyone and are never ranked.

docs.title: defaults/positions.yaml and positions.yaml
docs.text:
defaults/positions.yaml ships with four positions about an organization's own leadership. positions.yaml is yours and ships empty.

positions:
  Leader:            {titles: [boss, leader, head of organization]}
  Second-in-command: {below: [Leader], titles: [second in command, deputy]}
  Member:            {below: [Second-in-command, Leader], titles: [member, crew member]}
  Associate:         {outside: true, titles: [associate, close associate, contact]}

A position you name in positions.yaml that also exists in the defaults keeps its generic titles and adds yours. It keeps its generic place in the ladder too, unless your entry gives its own below or above, which then replace the generic ones.

So mapping your data's wording onto a default rank is one line, and nothing moves: Leader: {titles: [administrator, chair]} makes "administrator" and "chair" rank as Leader. Keep the wording in the records as the source has it; the title does the mapping.

A new name in positions.yaml simply adds a position, and it can sit under a generic one (below: [Leader]). The demo archive, for instance, moves Member down a level:

Member: {below: [Crew chief, Head of security, Second-in-command]}

To start from nothing, switch the generic positions off with hydra-ctl defaults off generic, and positions.yaml is the whole ladder. The shipped hints.yaml still gives icons to Leader and Second-in-command, so check warns hints.unknown-position until you point those two rules at your own ranks (match: {position: Boss}) or remove them.

docs.title: Labelling strategies
docs.text:
If your data's roles don't line up with the hierarchy, you have a few options:

  1. Label your positions using existing labels in the hierarchy.
  2. Modify the hierarchy to fit your data.
  3. Add the wording your data uses as a title on an existing position.

It's reasonable to gather some data first, then shape positions.yaml after.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Build once and look at the titles your data uses. 
    hydra-ctl build
hydra-ctl positions --unplaced
    This lists every role and position wording found in the data that no position takes yet. These are your raw material.
  2. Sketch the ladder top down. One name per rank, then, for each rank, the wordings from step 1 that mean it.
  3. Write positions.yaml. In each below, name only the rank directly above.
  4. Check the files. 
    hydra-ctl check
    It reports a title claimed by two positions (positions.title-twice; the first position wins), a misspelled key, or an outside position with a below.
  5. Build and read the ladder. 
    hydra-ctl build
hydra-ctl positions --tree --nodes
    The ladder shows each position, its titles and who holds it. Problems the ladder itself has are listed at the end under issues: a position named in a below that you never defined, or a loop (A below B, B below A), which Hydra cuts.
  6. Look at the tree. 
    hydra-ctl tree
hydra-ctl positions --unplaced
    Each record now sits under its rank. Anything still listed by --unplaced is a wording you haven't given a position, which may be fine (not every role is a rank) or an alias to add.
  7. Review the placements. hydra-ctl review --only placements asks about each placement the rules made. a keeps every placement one rule made at once, a number picks another parent, and your answers stay through later builds.

Repeat steps 3 to 7 as the data grows.

docs.title: Rules that keep a hierarchy valid
docs.text: Name one rank in below. Staff: {below: [Vice president]} falls back to the chief executive on its own when there is no vice president. Staff: {below: [Vice president, Chief executive]} puts both on the same level, and the first in alphabetical order wins: staff end up under the chief executive. Give each title to one position. If two positions claim "director", the first wins and check warns. Define every position you name. A below that names an undefined position creates an empty "implied" one and an issue. No loops. If A is below B and B below A, Hydra cuts one link and reports it. Keep separate chains separate. A company and a criminal crew need different rank names and titles. Ranks with the same name are one rank everywhere in the archive. Watch organization memberships. An organization whose Membership role is a position title is ranked like a person: a unit that is a "member" of an agency goes under the agency's Leader. For one organization inside another, use a role that is not a rank, such as "affiliate", "unit" or "branch", or leave the role blank. Add other languages as aliases. titles: [boss, jefe, capo]. Accents are already ignored, so líder matches lider. Quote values with commas, colons or #. Inside {…}, write titles: ["head, operations"], or YAML splits the value. Icons go elsewhere. positions.yaml only holds positions. Icons and badges by position go in hints.yaml (match: {position: Lieutenant}).

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Each of these has been built and checked with Hydra. None is on by default. To use one, paste its block below at the end of .hydra/rules/positions.yaml (the shipped file holds only comments), add your data's wordings to the titles, then run hydra-ctl check and hydra-ctl build.

docs.title: A criminal organization
docs.text:
Its titles overlap the generic positions, so switch those off first: hydra-ctl defaults off generic

Boss:        {titles: [boss, leader, don, kingpin]}
Underboss:   {below: [Boss], titles: [underboss, second in command]}
Lieutenant:  {below: [Underboss], titles: [lieutenant, capo, captain]}
Soldier:     {below: [Lieutenant], titles: [soldier, enforcer, crew member]}
Lawyer:      {outside: true, titles: [lawyer, attorney, consigliere]}

docs.title: A company
docs.text:
Kept apart from the generic Leader chain:

Chief executive: {titles: [ceo, chief executive officer, president, managing director]}
Vice president:  {below: [Chief executive], titles: [vice president, vp, v.p., senior vice president]}
Staff:           {below: [Vice president], titles: [staff, analyst, engineer, manager]}
Board member:    {outside: true, titles: [director, board member, chairman]}

The board sits beside the chain, so board members never rank staff, and staff never rank under a director. The defaults leave corporate ranks out on purpose: one shared ladder for every kind of relationship put employees under board members and companies under people.

docs.title: A government agency
docs.text:
Agency director:          {titles: [director, administrator, commissioner]}
Deputy director:          {below: [Agency director], titles: [deputy director, deputy administrator]}
Special agent in charge:  {below: [Deputy director], titles: [special agent in charge, sac, field office head]}
Special agent:            {below: [Special agent in charge], titles: [special agent, agent, investigator]}

With records whose roles say "Administrator", "Deputy Administrator", "SAC" and "special agent", this draws (the also lines left out):

Federal Customs Agency (PublicBody)
└── Dana Hale (Person) — Agency director
    └── Rob Kerr (Person) — Deputy director
        └── Lia Ortiz (Person) — Special agent in charge
            └── Sam Webb (Person) — Special agent

A fifth role in the same data, "Task Force Officer", shows up in positions --unplaced until you give it a position.

The company and agency recipes both use "director" for different ranks. In one archive, pick one meaning per title.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text:
An agent building a hierarchy should follow the steps above, reading Hydra's own output instead of guessing:

  • Read the titles in use: hydra-ctl positions --unplaced --format json returns {"unrelated": [...], "issues": [...]}. Only give positions to wordings that appear there. Never invent titles the data doesn't use.
  • Read the current ladder: hydra-ctl positions --format json.
  • Write only positions.yaml. Leave defaults/positions.yaml and direction.yaml as shipped unless the person asks.
  • Validate before finishing: hydra-ctl check must show no errors and no positions.* or hints.unknown-position warnings, and after hydra-ctl build, hydra-ctl positions --format json must return "issues": [].
  • Leave the decisions to the person. Don't answer review questions on their behalf. A hierarchy proposes placements, and the person confirms them.

docs.title: Images and badges
docs.text:
Hints link icons, portraits, logos and badges to entities by the entities' own data. Records never name their own image, and position files never hold media.

The rules live in .hydra/rules/hints.yaml, and the images in .hydra/resources/. The quickest way to add one is hints set, which copies the image in and writes the rule for you:

hydra-ctl hints set portrait ~/pics/pollard.webp --schema Person --name "Jonathan Jay Pollard"
hydra-ctl hints set thumb icons/crown.svg --position Analyst

docs.title: hints.yaml
docs.text:
hints:
  - match: {position: Analyst}
    set:   {thumb: icons/crown.svg}
  - match: {schema: Person, name: Jonathan Jay Pollard}
    set:   {portrait: portraits/pollard.webp}
  - match: {schema: PublicBody, name: Task Force 168}
    set:   {logo: portraits/tf168.webp}
  - match: {titled: {contains: "fighter pilot|secretary"}}
    set:   {thumb: icons/briefcase.svg}

Image paths are inside .hydra/resources/. A path that leaves it is refused, and check reports it.

The images above are examples. Only icons/crown.svg, icons/briefcase.svg, icons/public-body.svg and icons/star-2.svg ship; add your own with hydra-ctl hints set.

docs.title: Matching
docs.text:
A rule can match a schema, a position, or any field. name: means the name only; write name|alias: (or name|weakAlias:) to reach aliases too, since an alias can be shared by someone else.

titled: matches a title the data itself states. That is the entity's own position, the role on a relationship where it is the member, employee, director, owner or holder (never the other end), or the name and aliases of a post it holds.

A default such as "Member" for a membership with no role is never a stated title. A titled: rule only changes what is shown; it never sets a position.

docs.title: Rules add up
docs.text:
Images add up instead of replacing each other. Every matching rule adds its thumb, portrait or logo to the entity's list, in file order, with the rule and the field that matched, so a viewer can cycle through them.

The last badge set is the main one, and the others stay listed.

docs.title: Quoting
docs.text:
Quote a value that contains a comma, a colon or a # when it sits inside {…}. Unquoted, YAML splits {name: Dana Hale (no role, position Clerk)} at the comma, so the rule looks for a name of "Gale (no role" and matches nobody.

check flags the stray key that comes out. Write it as {name: "Dana Hale (no role, position Clerk)"}.

docs.title: Checking what matched
docs.text:
hydra-ctl hints

   0  {position: Leader}   {thumb: icons/crown.svg}   images on 5
   1  {position: Guard}   {thumb: icons/shield.svg}   images on 4
   2  {position: Clerk}   {thumb: icons/pen.svg}   images on 3
   …

Rules are numbered the way check names them (hints[4]), with how many nodes each one put an image on in the last build.

docs.title: hydra-mcp
docs.text:
hydra-mcp (source on GitHub) is an MCP server that lets an AI assistant turn a file into records for a Hydra archive. The assistant reads the file, writes the facts as Hydra's FollowTheMoney JSON, and the server checks them and saves them with the file as the evidence every entity cites.

It doesn't guess. Anything uncertain is left for a person: a name that might be someone already in the archive becomes a merge question in hydra-ctl review, and a role the hierarchy doesn't rank is reported, not rewritten.

docs.title: How a session goes
docs.text:
1. labelling_guidelines tells the assistant how to model records for this archive.
  2. read_file returns the file's text, exactly as it will be stored.
  3. describe_schema shows the properties and types of each kind of record, and find_entities looks each name up, so records reuse the exact name of anyone already in the archive.
  4. check_records is a dry run: it reports errors, warnings and how each link and role resolves, and writes nothing.
  5. save checks the records again, writes them and rebuilds. If anything breaks the modelling rules, nothing is written and errors says what to fix.
  6. get_records reads the saved collection back, with each property's type and what every link resolved to, so the assistant can check its work against the file.

You then answer whatever it left open with hydra-ctl todo and hydra-ctl review.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool Arguments What it does labelling_guidelines archive The record format, which field each end of a relationship goes in, roles, dates, and this archive's relationship fields and position ladder read_file path, offset, archive The text of a .txt, .md, .html, .pdf or .docx file. Long files come in parts: call again with offset set to next_offset. Says whether the archive already holds the file describe_schema schema, archive With no schema, the record types and relationships. With one, every property it accepts: its type, whether it is required, and what a link takes find_entities query, schema, limit, archive Entities already in the archive closest to a name, best first check_records records, collection, archive A dry run of save: errors, warnings, how links and roles resolve, likely duplicates. Writes nothing save records, source, collection, replace, archive Checks and saves records as a new collection with their evidence, then rebuilds get_records collection, name, offset, limit, archive Reads a saved collection back with each property's type, what each link resolved to after the build, and the save checks repeated. With no collection, lists them link_image image, kind, schema, position, titled, name, confirm, archive Previews, then on confirm=true adds, a hints rule giving matching entities a portrait, an icon (thumb) or a logo create_archive path, name, prefix, confirm Previews, then on confirm=true creates, an empty archive in a new or empty folder (as hydra-ctl init). prefix defaults to one made from the name; none gives each collection its own

path arguments must be full paths. A scanned PDF with no text layer is an error, never an empty source.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Records use Hydra's dialect: links are written as the linked entity's name, not an id. See Links.

[
  {
    "schema": "Person",
    "properties": {
      "name": [
        "Rob Kerr"
      ],
      "weakAlias": [
        "Kerr"
      ]
    }
  },
  {
    "schema": "PublicBody",
    "properties": {
      "name": [
        "Port Authority"
      ]
    }
  },
  {
    "schema": "Employment",
    "properties": {
      "employee": [
        "Rob Kerr"
      ],
      "employer": [
        "Port Authority"
      ],
      "role": [
        "deputy"
      ],
      "startDate": [
        "2019"
      ]
    }
  }
]

id is optional. Dates are YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: The source argument of save
docs.text:
{"file": "/full/path/report.pdf"} keeps the file as the evidence, {"text": "..."} keeps pasted text, and {"id": "..."} adds more records from evidence already saved. A file already saved in the archive is refused; save with its id instead.

Add title, url (which makes the source an Article), publisher, author, published or language when known.

docs.title: Images
docs.text: Records never carry images. link_image adds a rule to .hydra/rules/hints.yaml instead, the same rule hydra-ctl hints set writes. It only previews until it is called with confirm=true, which the assistant should do only after you agree. See Images and badges.

docs.title: What a save writes
docs.text:
collections/<collection>.json                  the records
.hydra/sources/entries/<collection>.json       the source, as one Document
.hydra/sources/files/<collection>/<file>       a copy of the original file

Every entity cites the source in sources, so hydra-ctl claims and hydra-ctl sources trace each value back to the file. Relationships have no sources field in FtM; they trace back through their collection.

The collection is named from the file or title plus a timestamp unless you pass collection, and an existing one is never overwritten unless replace=true. If the rebuild fails, the files are put back as they were.

To undo a save, delete the files it lists in undo, then run hydra-ctl build.

docs.title: Choosing the archive
docs.text:
The archive is, in order: the tool's archive argument, the HYDRA_ARCHIVE environment variable, an archive activated with hydra-ctl activate in or above the folder the server starts in, or that folder if it is an archive.

With no archive, nothing is written. labelling_guidelines, read_file, describe_schema and check_records still work on Hydra's defaults, find_entities returns nothing, and save, get_records and link_image refuse and tell the assistant to ask you for a folder or offer create_archive.

A path that is named but isn't an archive is an error, never a quiet fallback.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
hydra-mcp is a Python package with a hydra-mcp command, like hydra-ctl. It depends on open-hydra, the main open-hydra package. Neither is on PyPI, so install both from GitHub in one go:

uv tool install git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra-mcp --with git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra

Or with pip, into any environment:

pip install git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra git+https://github.com/meridiangray/open-hydra-mcp

Afterwards hydra-mcp is on your PATH. It speaks MCP over stdio, so running it by hand just waits for a client.

docs.title: 2. Add it to your client
docs.text:
Every MCP client needs the same two things: the command hydra-mcp, and optionally HYDRA_ARCHIVE set to the archive's folder. Leave HYDRA_ARCHIVE out to choose the archive per conversation.

Claude Code:

claude mcp add hydra --env HYDRA_ARCHIVE=/path/to/case -- hydra-mcp

Add --scope user to make it available in every project, or --scope project to write it to .mcp.json for everyone working in the repo.

Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code and other clients take the standard mcpServers JSON. For Claude Desktop it goes in claude_desktop_config.json (Settings → Developer → Edit Config):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "hydra": {
      "command": "hydra-mcp",
      "env": {"HYDRA_ARCHIVE": "/path/to/case"}
    }
  }
}

Restart the client, and the tools appear under hydra.

If the client can't find the command, give its full path instead. which hydra-mcp (macOS, Linux) or where hydra-mcp (Windows) prints it.

Windows: give the full path and double every backslash:

"command": "C:\\Users\\you\\.local\\bin\\hydra-mcp.exe",
"env": {"HYDRA_ARCHIVE": "C:\\cases\\case"}

Installed in WSL, client on Windows:

"command": "wsl",
"args": ["-d", "Debian", "--", "bash", "-lc", "HYDRA_ARCHIVE=/mnt/c/cases/case hydra-mcp"]

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: To update, run the install again with uv tool install --reinstall (or pip install --force-reinstall) and restart the client.

docs.title: Reviewing
docs.text:
Hydra assumes your fields are correct, then asks you about what it can't settle itself: records that might be one entity, names that could mean several records, and records with more than one possible parent.

hydra-ctl todo              # count what is open, by kind
hydra-ctl todo --list       # each question with its id
hydra-ctl review            # answer them one by one

  kind             open
  merges              0
  references          0
  placements          2
  stale               0
  contradictions      0
  verdicts            0

The demo asks only two placement questions. The merge and reference screens below come from adding a second collection that names the same man differently (press.json: "Jonathan Pollard", and a link that says only "Jonathan").

Each answer is saved at once to .hydra/review/verdicts.yaml, and the archive is rebuilt once at the end. hydra-ctl review --only placements asks just one kind.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text: Key Does a number Picks that answer ? or Enter Leaves the question open u Undoes the last answer q Stops a On a placement made by the position rules, keeps every placement that rule made Tab / Shift+Tab Rotates the view between all fields, fields in both, and conflicting fields

docs.title: Merges
docs.text:
A merge asks whether two records are one entity or two. A merge with a conflict opens on just the conflicting fields, since that is what you have to decide. Here two records might be one man:

[1/1] Merge
  Jonathan Pollard   and   Jonathan Jay Pollard

  pollard:per-k3m8v1qz5t   Person
     alias       Jay Pollard
     birthDate   1954
     name        Jonathan Pollard
     notes       Navy analyst, arrested in 1985

  pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe   Person
     alias       Jonathan Pollard
     name        Jonathan Jay Pollard
     sources     pollard:doc-v9g25vcmkx
     weakAlias   Pollard

  [all fields]   fields in both   conflicting fields      Tab / Shift+Tab
Which is better?
  1  one entity
  2  two entities
  ? not sure   u undo   q quit

Press Tab to see every field of both records, with = for the same and ≠ for the conflict.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
A link written as a name that fits more than one record is asked as a reference. Here, which record does the Employment record mean by "Jonathan"?

[1/1] Reference · a name with 2 possible records
  pollard:emp-b7d2n9x4hc   Employment.employee   Jonathan

  ┌─ Link from ───────────────────────────────┐
  │ pollard:emp-b7d2n9x4hc   Employment       │
  │  → employee   Jonathan                    │
  │    employer   Naval Investigative Service │
  │    role       analyst                     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  1  pollard:per-k3m8v1qz5t   Person
     alias       Jay Pollard
     birthDate   1954
     name        Jonathan Pollard
     notes       Navy analyst, arrested in 1985

  2  pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe   Person
     alias       Jonathan Pollard
     name        Jonathan Jay Pollard
     sources     pollard:doc-v9g25vcmkx
     weakAlias   Pollard

  [all fields]   name fields   matching fields      Tab / Shift+Tab
Which record is "Jonathan"?
  1  Jonathan Pollard       pollard:per-k3m8v1qz5t
  2  Jonathan Jay Pollard   pollard:per-w3v2f7z7pe
  3  neither
  ? not sure   u undo   q quit

docs.title: Placements
docs.text:
When the rules put a record under one parent and the data offers another, you pick the one the tree draws. Picking a keeps every placement made by the same rule.

[1/2] Placement · Membership (several parents)
  Jonathan Jay Pollard
  …
Which is better?
  1  under Task Force 168                                pollard:org-ctk7r6bt77   now
  2  under Anti-Terrorist Alert Center                   pollard:org-8b2fsev104
  3  under Naval Ocean Surveillance Information Center   pollard:org-3kk63smvp7
  4  under Navy Field Operational Intelligence Office    pollard:org-1phejc0ngk
  ? not sure   u undo   q quit

Choosing an organization puts the record inside it. The position rules then decide who it sits under there, and never move it out of that organization.

The data in the entity's fields does not change. A placement only decides how the tree is drawn.

docs.title: Stale decisions and contradictions
docs.text: A merge decision is saved with its evidence, so it comes back as stale if that evidence changes. A contradiction is a value the sources disagree on. Both are asked after the merges, references and placements.

docs.title: Leftover decisions
docs.text:
A decision whose question no longer exists (the records it was made on changed) is asked again, so you can drop it or keep it:

[1/1] Decision problem
  verdicts.orphan: no ledger row has this key (the records it decided may have changed)
Which is better?
  1  remove that decision
  2  keep it                   now
  ? not sure   u undo   q quit

docs.title: Undoing decisions
docs.text: hydra-ctl answer <id> clear clears one decision. reset removes many at once, after backing up verdicts.yaml.

docs.title: The tree after review
docs.text:
After you reject Task Force 168 as his parent, the tree draws him under another and says why the first isn't the one:

hydra-ctl answer place-… reject
hydra-ctl tree pollard

Jonathan Jay Pollard (Person) — Analyst
  also  Anti-Terrorist Alert Center                  Employment   analyst
  also  Navy Field Operational Intelligence Office   Employment   analyst
  also  Task Force 168                               Membership             rejected
Anne Henderson-Pollard (Person)

Each also line is another parent the record has. A word at the end says why it isn't the drawn one, such as rejected for a parent you turned down; see tree.

docs.title: hydra.yaml
docs.text:
The archive's own settings.

Key Is name The archive's name, asked by init prefix The id prefix every collection uses unless it has its own, asked by init ftm The hash of the FollowTheMoney schema the archive was made with; every export is stamped with it defaults_off The default rule files you switched off with hydra-ctl defaults off subject Optional. Names the organization the archive charts search Optional. Sets how far searches look when no flag says: all (the default), no-text (every field but free text) or names (names and ids) format The archive layout's version, written by init

docs.title: .hydra/rules/
docs.text:
positions.yaml is your archive's own hierarchy, and defaults/positions.yaml holds the generic positions it builds on. Both are covered in Defining Hierarchies.

hints.yaml links icons, portraits, logos and badges to entities; see Images and badges.

docs.title: .hydra/review/verdicts.yaml
docs.text:
Written by hydra-ctl review and hydra-ctl answer: one line per decision (this merge confirmed, that placement rejected). It is read on every build and travels with the archive.

hydra-ctl reset removes decisions, after backing the file up.

docs.title: .hydra/schema/
docs.text:
The FollowTheMoney schema the archive uses, and Hydra's settings for it. These are background configuration: you can change them, but probably shouldn't. hydra-ctl defaults checks and restores params/, direction.yaml and the extensions/ files. It doesn't touch ftm/; to restore that, see open-hydra-schema.

Path Is ftm/followthemoney/ The FtM schema itself (types, properties, relationships) ftm/config/ FtM's own config files params/ One file per type (Person.param.yaml…) direction.yaml Which end of each relationship is the parent extensions/collate.yaml A helper for hierarchies and reviews extensions/artifact.yaml Hydra's extension types

docs.title: params
docs.text: Each param file says which fields decide that two records are the same entity (match), which fields keep them apart when they disagree (distinct), and which fields place a record under another (fold). A list in a param file replaces Hydra's defaults for that category.

docs.title: direction.yaml
docs.text:
Says which end of each kind of relationship is the higher one: an Ownership's owner is above what it owns, a Membership's organization above its member. Some relationships are marked sideways (family, associates, lawyers), and those never make a hierarchy.

It is a helper for some annoying logic: leave it alone. It is also where edge_positions lives, the opt-in that fills a title in for a role-less Membership, Employment or Directorship.

docs.title: artifact.yaml
docs.text: extensions/artifact.yaml (with collate.yaml) holds extension types: Hydra's additions to FtM, such as the sources field on every entity and notes on relationships.
